topic.1.step.ball.title: The Earth is a ball
topic.1.step.ball.body: To say exactly where a place is on a ball, we draw an imaginary grid on it. The grid has two kinds of lines: parallels and meridians. Drag the globe to turn it.
topic.1.step.equator.title: The equator
topic.1.step.equator.body: The equator goes around the middle of the Earth. It is the longest parallel and its latitude is 0°. It divides the Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.
topic.1.step.parallels.title: Parallels
topic.1.step.parallels.body: Parallels are circles that run parallel to the equator. The closer to a pole, the shorter they are. They tell us the latitude: from 0° at the equator up to 90°N at the North Pole or 90°S at the South Pole.
topic.1.step.angle.title: Why degrees?
topic.1.step.angle.body: Latitude is an angle! Imagine a line from the centre of the Earth to a place. The angle between that line and the equator is the latitude. Drag the point on the circle and watch the angle change.
topic.1.step.meridians.title: Meridians
topic.1.step.meridians.body: Meridians are half-circles that join the North Pole and the South Pole. All meridians are the same length. They tell us the longitude.
topic.1.step.prime.title: The prime meridian and 180°
topic.1.step.prime.body: The prime meridian (0°) goes through Greenwich in London. On the other side of the Earth is the 180° meridian. Together they divide the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Longitude goes from 0° up to 180°E or 180°W.
topic.1.step.projections.title: Many maps, one grid
topic.1.step.projections.body: A flat map is always a little stretched, because the Earth is round. This map is called Equal Earth: every country keeps its true size, so the meridians bend. The coordinates stay the same on every map. Try the Grid map in the Lab to compare.
topic.1.step.tropics.title: Tropics and polar circles
topic.1.step.tropics.body: Some parallels have their own names: the Tropic of Cancer (about 23°N), the Tropic of Capricorn (about 23°S), the Arctic Circle (about 66°N) and the Antarctic Circle (about 66°S).
topic.1.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.1.step.play.body: Drag the point around. When is it in the Northern Hemisphere? When is it in the Western Hemisphere? Find the Tropic of Cancer.
topic.2.step.north-south.title: North or south?
topic.2.step.north-south.body: On a map, north is at the top. Warsaw (52°N) is north of the 50°N parallel. Rome (42°N) is south of it. In the Northern Hemisphere a bigger number means further north.
topic.2.step.southern.title: Careful in the south!
topic.2.step.southern.body: In the Southern Hemisphere a bigger number means further south. 40°S is south of 20°S, and 10°S is north of it.
topic.2.step.east-west.title: East or west?
topic.2.step.east-west.body: East is to the right on a map. Kyiv (31°E) is east of the 20°E meridian. London (0°) is west of it. In the Eastern Hemisphere a bigger number means further east.
topic.2.step.western.title: Careful in the west!
topic.2.step.western.body: In the Western Hemisphere a bigger number means further west. 100°W is west of 60°W, and 30°W is east of it.
topic.2.step.across-zero.title: Across the lines
topic.2.step.across-zero.body: Every place with N latitude is north of every place with S latitude. Every place with E longitude is east of Greenwich, and every place with W longitude is west of it.
topic.2.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.2.step.play.body: Move the point and say it out loud: is it north or south of the equator? East or west of Greenwich? Then check the coordinates below the map.
topic.3.step.address.title: An address in two numbers
topic.3.step.address.body: Coordinates are written as latitude first, then longitude: 52°N, 21°E. That is Warsaw!
topic.3.step.latitude.title: Step 1: latitude
topic.3.step.latitude.body: Find the parallel that goes through the point and read its number at the left edge of the map. Is the point above the equator (N) or below it (S)?
topic.3.step.longitude.title: Step 2: longitude
topic.3.step.longitude.body: Now find the meridian that goes through the point and read its number at the bottom edge. Is the point right of Greenwich (E) or left of it (W)?
topic.3.step.answer.title: Put it together
topic.3.step.answer.body: The point lies on the 30°N parallel and on the 30°E meridian. Its coordinates are 30°N, 30°E — very close to Cairo.
topic.3.step.between.title: Between the lines
topic.3.step.between.body: If a point lies between two lines, count the degrees. Halfway between 40° and 50° is 45°.
topic.3.step.southwest.title: South and west
topic.3.step.southwest.body: Try this point yourself: which parallel and which meridian go through it? Remember the letters S and W. (Answer: 30°S, 60°W.)
topic.3.step.globe.title: On the globe
topic.3.step.globe.body: The grid works the same way on the globe. Turn the globe to find the point near Sydney: 34°S, 151°E.
topic.3.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.3.step.play.body: Drag the point, say its coordinates out loud, then check the answer below the map.
topic.4.step.plan.title: From numbers to a place
topic.4.step.plan.body: Let's find 50°N, 30°E. First find the parallel: 50°N.
topic.4.step.meridian.title: Then the meridian
topic.4.step.meridian.body: Now find the meridian 30°E. Remember: E means to the right of Greenwich.
topic.4.step.cross.title: Where the lines cross
topic.4.step.cross.body: The place is where the two lines cross. It is Kyiv!
topic.4.step.letters.title: Letters matter
topic.4.step.letters.body: 34°S, 151°E is Sydney. But 34°N, 151°W is in the middle of the Pacific Ocean! Always check N or S and E or W.
topic.4.step.play.title: Try it yourself
topic.4.step.play.body: Drag the point to find places, or pick a city from the list and check its coordinates.

places.title: Places
q.nameLine.promptPoint: In which two hemispheres is point A?
q.nameLine.explain.equator: The equator is the parallel 0°. It runs around the middle of the Earth.
q.nameLine.explain.prime: The prime meridian is 0°. It goes through Greenwich in London.
q.nameLine.explain.antimeridian: The 180° meridian is on the opposite side of the Earth from Greenwich.
q.nameLine.explain.parallel: This is the parallel {value}. Parallels are circles parallel to the equator.
q.nameLine.explain.meridian: This is the meridian {value}. Meridians join the North Pole and the South Pole.
q.nameLine.explain.tropicCancer: The Tropic of Cancer is the parallel at about 23½°N.
q.nameLine.explain.tropicCapricorn: The Tropic of Capricorn is the parallel at about 23½°S.
q.nameLine.explain.arcticCircle: The Arctic Circle is the parallel at about 66½°N.
q.nameLine.explain.antarcticCircle: The Antarctic Circle is the parallel at about 66½°S.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.N: The Northern Hemisphere is everything north of the equator.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.S: The Southern Hemisphere is everything south of the equator.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.E: The Eastern Hemisphere is everything east of the prime meridian, up to 180°.
q.nameLine.explainHemi.W: The Western Hemisphere is everything west of the prime meridian, up to 180°.
q.nameLine.explainPoint: Point A is at {coords}, so it is in the {nsHemi} and {ewHemi} hemispheres.
q.further.mistake.opposite: That point lies furthest {dir} — the opposite direction!
q.rule.mixed.lat: Any place with N latitude is north of any place with S latitude.
q.rule.mixed.lon: Any place with E longitude is east of any place with W longitude (as long as we do not cross the 180° meridian).
q.rule.bigger.N: In the Northern Hemisphere, a bigger number means further north.
q.rule.bigger.S: In the Southern Hemisphere, a bigger number means further south.
q.rule.bigger.E: In the Eastern Hemisphere, a bigger number means further east.
q.rule.bigger.W: In the Western Hemisphere, a bigger number means further west.
q.rule.zero.lat: Places with N latitude lie north of the equator (0°), places with S latitude lie south of it.
q.rule.zero.lon: Places with E longitude lie east of the prime meridian (0°), places with W longitude lie west of it.
q.relative.prompt.lat: Is point A ({point}) north or south of the parallel {line}?
q.relative.prompt.lon: Is point A ({point}) east or west of the meridian {line}?
q.relative.explain.lat: Point A has latitude {value} and the parallel is {line}, so the point lies {dir} of the parallel. {rule}
q.relative.explain.lon: Point A has longitude {value} and the meridian is {line}, so the point lies {dir} of the meridian. {rule}
q.read.prompt: What are the coordinates of the point?
q.read.explain: The point lies on the parallel {lat} and on the meridian {lon}, so its coordinates are {coords}.
q.place.explain: First find the parallel {lat}, then the meridian {lon}. The point goes where they cross.
q.mistake.nsLetter: Check the letter: N means north of the equator, S means south of it.
q.mistake.ewLetter: Check the letter: E means east of Greenwich, W means west of it.
q.mistake.bothLetters: Both letters are the wrong way round. N or S says up or down, E or W says right or left.
q.mistake.swapped: Latitude and longitude are swapped. Latitude (N or S) always comes first.
q.mistake.minutes: Close! Check the minutes: 30′ is half a degree and 15′ is a quarter of a degree.
